title: Heterogeneous Defect Prediction (Nam, Fu, Kim, Menzies, Tan; IEEE TSE submission 2016)

edges.target: CPDP-IFS (He, Li, Ma)
edges.ref: [46] P. He, B. Li, and Y. Ma, Towards cross-project defect prediction with imbalanced feature sets, CoRR abs/1411.4228, 2014
edges.evidence: We include CPDP-IFS proposed by He et al. as a baseline [46]. ... the approach by He et al. is not compared with WPDP ... the evaluation might be weak

edges.target: CPDP using common metrics / NN filter (Turhan et al.)
edges.ref: [14] Turhan, Menzies, Bener, Di Stefano, On the relative value of cross-company and within-company data for defect prediction, ESE, 2009
edges.evidence: We conduct CPDP using only common metrics (CPDP-CM) between source and target datasets as in previous CPDP studies [12], [14], [46]

edges.target: Transfer Naive Bayes / common-metric CPDP (Ma et al.)
edges.ref: [12] Y. Ma, G. Luo, X. Zeng, A. Chen, Transfer learning for cross-company software defect prediction, Inf. Softw. Technol. 54(3), 2012
edges.evidence: Since using common metrics has been adopted to address the limitation on heterogeneous metric sets in previous CPDP studies [12], [14], [46], we set CPDP-CM as a baseline

edges.target: CCA+ heterogeneous cross-company defect prediction (Jing et al.)
edges.ref: [47] Jing, Wu, Dong, Qi, Xu, Heterogeneous cross-company defect prediction by unified metric representation and cca-based transfer learning, FSE'15
edges.evidence: the implementation of CCA+ is not publicly available yet and more complex than HDP ... CCA+ transforms original source and target datasets so that it is difficult to directly explain

edges.target: HDP conference version (Nam & Kim, FSE 2015)
edges.ref: [16] J. Nam and S. Kim, Heterogeneous defect prediction, ESEC/FSE 2015, pp. 508-519
edges.evidence: We extend the previous conference paper of the same name [16] in the following ways.

edges.target: Kolmogorov-Smirnov test (Massey)
edges.ref: [55] F. J. Massey, The kolmogorov-smirnov test for goodness of fit, JASA 46(253), pp. 68-78, 1951
edges.evidence: KSAnalyzer uses a p-value from the Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test (KS-test) as a matching score between source and target metrics.

edges.target: KS-test applicability without normality (Lilliefors)
edges.ref: [58] H. W. Lilliefors, On the kolmogorov-smirnov test for normality with mean and variance unknown, JASA 62(318), 1967
edges.evidence: The KS-test is a non-parametric two sample test that can be applicable when we cannot be sure about the normality of two samples and/or the same variance [55], [58].

edges.target: Spearman rank correlation
edges.ref: [56] C. Spearman, The proof and measurement of association between two things, Int. J. Epidemiology 39(5), 2010
edges.evidence: In SCoAnalyzer, we used the Spearman's rank correlation coefficient as a matching score for source and target metrics [56].

edges.target: Cliff's delta with Romano et al. magnitude thresholds
edges.ref: [73] J. Romano, J. D. Kromrey, J. Coraggio, J. Skowronek, Appropriate statistics for ordinal level data..., Florida Assoc. Inst. Research, 2006
edges.evidence: we compute Cliff's delta that is a non-parametric effect size measure [73]. As Romano et al. suggested, we evaluate the magnitude of the effect size as follows: negligible (|d| < 0.147)

edges.target: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
edges.ref: [77] F. Wilcoxon, Individual Comparisons by Ranking Methods, Biometrics Bulletin 1(6), pp. 80-83, 1945
edges.evidence: we conduct the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (p<0.05) for all AUC values in baselines and HDP [77].

edges.target: Win/Tie/Loss evaluation (Kocaguneli, Menzies et al.)
edges.ref: [74] E. Kocaguneli, T. Menzies, J. Keung, D. Cok, R. Madachy, Active learning and effort estimation..., IEEE TSE 39(8), 2013
edges.evidence: we also use the Win/Tie/Loss evaluation, which is used for performance comparison between different experimental settings in many studies [74], [75], [76].

edges.target: Win/Tie/Loss evaluation (Li et al.)
edges.ref: [75] M. Li, H. Zhang, R. Wu, Z.-H. Zhou, Sample-based software defect prediction with active and semi-supervised learning, ASE 19(2), 2012
edges.evidence: we also use the Win/Tie/Loss evaluation, which is used for performance comparison between different experimental settings in many studies [74], [75], [76].

edges.target: Win/Tie/Loss evaluation (Valentini & Dietterich)
edges.ref: [76] G. Valentini and T. G. Dietterich, Low bias bagged support vector machines, ICML 2003, pp. 752-759
edges.evidence: we also use the Win/Tie/Loss evaluation, which is used for performance comparison between different experimental settings in many studies [74], [75], [76].

edges.target: Repeat randomized experiments guideline (Arcuri & Briand)
edges.ref: [68] A. Arcuri and L. Briand, A practical guide for using statistical tests to assess randomized algorithms in software engineering, ICSE 2011
edges.evidence: We repeat these two rounds 500 times, i.e. 1000 tests, since there is a randomness in selecting instances for each split [68].

edges.target: Top-15% feature selection rule (Gao et al.)
edges.ref: [50] Gao, Khoshgoftaar, Wang, Seliya, Choosing software metrics for defect prediction: An investigation on feature selection techniques, SPE 2011
edges.evidence: When applying feature selection approaches, we select top 15% of metrics as suggested by Gao et al. [50].

edges.target: Feature selection for defect prediction (Shivaji, Whitehead, Akella, Kim)
edges.ref: [51] S. Shivaji, E. J. Whitehead, R. Akella, S. Kim, Reducing features to improve code change-based bug prediction, IEEE TSE 39(4), 2013
edges.evidence: we used various feature selection approaches widely used in defect prediction such as gain ratio, chi-square, relief-F, and significance attribute evaluation [50], [51].

edges.target: Maximum weighted bipartite matching
edges.ref: [57] J. Matousek and B. Gaertner, Understanding and Using Linear Programming (Universitext), Springer, 2006
edges.evidence: we used the maximum weighted bipartite matching [57] technique to select a group of matched metrics, whose sum of matching scores is highest, without duplicated metrics.

edges.target: AUC as defect-prediction measure (Rahman, Posnett, Devanbu)
edges.ref: [13] F. Rahman, D. Posnett, P. Devanbu, Recalling the imprecision of cross-project defect prediction, FSE 2012
edges.evidence: AUC is unaffected by class imbalance as well as being independent from the cutoff probability ... [13], [69], [70], [71] ... the AUC of 0.5 means the performance of a random predictor [13].

edges.target: AUC as benchmark measure (Lessmann et al.)
edges.ref: [70] S. Lessmann, B. Baesens, C. Mues, S. Pietsch, Benchmarking classification models for software defect prediction, IEEE TSE 34(4), 2008
edges.evidence: The AUC is known as a useful measure for comparing different models and is widely used because AUC is unaffected by class imbalance

edges.target: Cutoff-dependence problem in defect prediction comparisons (Mende)
edges.ref: [72] T. Mende, Replication of defect prediction studies: Problems, pitfalls and recommendations, PROMISE 2010
edges.evidence: Mende confirmed that it is difficult to compare the defect prediction performance reported in the defect prediction literature since prediction results come from the different cutoffs

edges.target: 50:50 random split protocol (TCA+, Nam et al.)
edges.ref: [8] J. Nam, S. J. Pan, S. Kim, Transfer defect learning, ICSE 2013, pp. 382-391
edges.evidence: We use 50:50 random splits, which are widely used in the evaluation of defect prediction models [8], [66], [67].

edges.target: 50:50 random split protocol (Pinzger et al.)
edges.ref: [67] M. Pinzger, N. Nagappan, B. Murphy, Can developer-module networks predict failures? FSE 2008, pp. 2-12
edges.evidence: We use 50:50 random splits, which are widely used in the evaluation of defect prediction models [8], [66], [67].

edges.target: AEEEM defect datasets (D'Ambros et al.)
edges.ref: [1] M. D'Ambros, M. Lanza, R. Robbes, Evaluating defect prediction approaches: a benchmark and an extensive comparison, ESE 17(4-5), 2012
edges.evidence: AEEEM was used to benchmark different defect prediction models [1] ... Each AEEEM dataset consists of 61 metrics

edges.target: ReLink defect datasets (Wu, Zhang, Kim, Cheung)
edges.ref: [59] R. Wu, H. Zhang, S. Kim, S. Cheung, Relink: Recovering links between bugs and changes, FSE 2011
edges.evidence: Datasets in ReLink were used by Wu et al. [59] to improve the defect prediction performance by increasing the quality of the defect data and have 26 code complexity metrics

edges.target: MORPH defect datasets (Peters & Menzies)
edges.ref: [60] F. Peters and T. Menzies, Privacy and utility for defect prediction: experiments with morph, ICSE 2012, pp. 189-199
edges.evidence: The MORPH group contains defect datasets of several open source projects used in the study about the dataset privacy issue for defect prediction [60].

edges.target: NASA defect datasets via PROMISE repository
edges.ref: [15] T. Menzies, B. Caglayan, Z. He, E. Kocaguneli, J. Krall, F. Peters, B. Turhan, The promise repository of empirical SE data, 2012
edges.evidence: We used five NASA datasets, which share the same metric set in the PROMISE repository [15], [61].

edges.target: Cleaned NASA datasets DS0 (Shepperd et al.)
edges.ref: [61] M. Shepperd, Q. Song, Z. Sun, C. Mair, Data quality: Some comments on the nasa software defect datasets, IEEE TSE 39(9), 2013
edges.evidence: We used cleaned NASA datasets (DS0 version) [61].

edges.target: SOFTLAB (Turkish company) datasets via PROMISE
edges.ref: [14] Turhan, Menzies, Bener, Di Stefano, On the relative value of cross-company and within-company data for defect prediction, ESE, 2009
edges.evidence: For the SOFTLAB group, we used all SOFTLAB datasets in the PROMISE repository [15].

edges.target: Weka (Logistic Regression and other learners)
edges.ref: [65] M. Hall, E. Frank, G. Holmes, B. Pfahringer, P. Reutemann, I. H. Witten, The weka data mining software: an update, SIGKDD Explor. 11, 2009
edges.evidence: We use Logistic Regression implemented in Weka with default options [65].

edges.target: Apache commons math (KolmogorovSmirnovTest, SpearmansCorrelation)
edges.ref: no reference entry; named in text as 'the Apache commons math library'
edges.evidence: We used the KolmogorovSmirnovTest implemented in the Apache commons math library.

edges.target: Understand static analysis tool (SciTools)
edges.ref: [62] Understand 2.0, http://www.scitools.com/products/
edges.evidence: have 26 code complexity metrics extracted by the Understand tool [62].

edges.target: Events-per-variable = 10 rule for logistic regression (Peduzzi et al.)
edges.ref: [84] Peduzzi, Concato, Kemper, Holford, Feinstein, A simulation study of the number of events per variable in logistic regression, J Clin Epidemiol...
edges.evidence: Peduzzi et al. [84] report 10 events per variable (EPV) are enough to maximize the predictive performance of Logistic Regression ... we picked 2 x 10 = 20 randomly selected defective data

edges.target: EPV analysis re-run on defect data (Peduzzi et al.)
edges.ref: [84] Peduzzi, Concato, Kemper, Holford, Feinstein, A simulation study of the number of events per variable in logistic regression, J Clin Epidemiol...
edges.evidence: For our defect datasets, in Figure 7, we repeated the analysis of [84] and found that ... there was little improvement after 100 examples with EPV = 10

edges.target: Probability of missing a signal after n trials (Voas & Miller)
edges.ref: [89] J. M. Voas and K. W. Miller, Software testability: The new verification, IEEE Software, no. 3, pp. 17-28, 1995
edges.evidence: According to Voas and Miller [89], if we see something at probability e, then we will miss it at probability 1 - e. After n attempts, the probability of missing it is (1 - e)^n

edges.target: Discretization policy in SE data mining (Menzies; Lustgarten et al.)
edges.ref: [87] Menzies, Data Mining, in Recommendation Systems in SE, 2014; [88] Lustgarten et al., Improving classification performance with discretization...
edges.evidence: it is common in data mining for SE [87] to divide dimensions accroding to some descritization policy [88]. Discretization converts a numeric variable with infinite range into a smaller number of b bins.

edges.target: Median-chop / two-bin defect predictors (Zhang et al. universal model; Nam & Kim CLAMI)
edges.ref: [85] Nam and Kim, Clami: Defect prediction on unlabeled datasets, ASE 2015; [45] Zhang et al., Towards building a universal defect prediction model...
edges.evidence: Recent results [45], [85] show that, for defect data, good predictors can be built via a median chop of numeric project data; they are divided into b = 2 bins

edges.target: Few dimensions needed for defect data (Menzies, Greenwald, Frank 2007)
edges.ref: [2] T. Menzies, J. Greenwald, A. Frank, Data mining static code attributes to learn defect predictors, IEEE TSE 33, pp. 2-13, 2007
edges.evidence: When applied to defect data [2], we found that those datasets may only need d in {2, 3} dimensions. ... good predictors can be built using d <= 7 of those dimensions [2]

edges.target: Correlated attributes in defect data (Shepperd & Ince)
edges.ref: [86] M. Shepperd and D. C. Ince, A Critique of Three Metrics, J. Systems and Software 26(3), pp. 197-210, 1994
edges.evidence: Other results [86] show that defect prediction data containing dozens of attributes, many of which are correlated attributes.

edges.target: Feature subset selection benchmark (Hall & Holmes)
edges.ref: [53] M. Hall and G. Holmes, Benchmarking attribute selection techniques for discrete class data mining, IEEE TKDE 15(6), 2003
edges.evidence: According to benchmark studies about various feature selection approaches, a single best feature selection approach for all prediction models does not exist [52], [53], [54].

edges.target: Common-metric CPDP f-measure 0.35 vs WPDP 0.39 (Turhan et al.)
edges.ref: [14] Turhan, Menzies, Bener, Di Stefano, On the relative value of cross-company and within-company data for defect prediction, ESE, 2009
edges.evidence: the CPDP approach proposed by Turhan et al. did not outperform WPDP in terms of the average f-measure (0.35 vs. 0.39) [14].

edges.target: Only 18% of PROMISE defect datasets share a metric set
edges.ref: [15] T. Menzies, B. Caglayan, Z. He, E. Kocaguneli, J. Krall, F. Peters, B. Turhan, The promise repository of empirical SE data, 2012
edges.evidence: at most 18% of defect datasets in the PROMISE repository have the same metric set [15].

edges.target: Static bug finders vs statistical prediction: no significant difference (Rahman et al. ICSE'14)
edges.ref: [36] F. Rahman, S. Khatri, E. Barr, P. Devanbu, Comparing static bug finders and statistical prediction, ICSE 2014, pp. 424-434
edges.evidence: They found no significant differences in the cost-effectiveness of these approaches.

edges.target: Defect predictors find 70% or more of defects (Menzies, Greenwald, Frank)
edges.ref: [31] T. Menzies, J. Greenwald, A. Frank, Data mining static code attributes to learn defect predictors, IEEE TSE 33(1), 2007
edges.evidence: Defect predictors often find the location of 70% (or more) of the defects in code [31].

edges.target: Manual reviews find about 60% of defects (IEEE Metrics 2002 panel)
edges.ref: [34] F. Shull, V. Basili, B. Boehm, et al., What we have learned about fighting defects, 8th Int. Software Metrics Symposium, 2002, pp. 249-258
edges.evidence: a panel at IEEE Metrics 2002 [34] concluded that manual software reviews can find about 60% of defects.

edges.target: Inspection defect detection 50% (Fagan) to 21% (Raffo)
edges.ref: [35] M. Fagan, Design and code inspections to reduce errors in program development, IBM Systems Journal 15(3), 1976
edges.evidence: Raffo documents the typical defect detection capability of industrial review methods: around 50% for full Fagan inspections [35] to 21% for less-structured inspections.

edges.target: Review rate 8-20 LOC/minute (Menzies, Raffo et al.)
edges.ref: [28] T. Menzies, D. Raffo, S. Setamanit, Y. Hu, S. Tootoonian, Model-based tests of truisms, ASE 2002
edges.evidence: depending on the review methods, 8 to 20 LOC/minute can be inspected and this effort repeats for all members of the review team, which can be as large as four or six people [28].

edges.target: CK metrics / RFC definition (Chidamber & Kemerer)
edges.ref: [80] S. R. Chidamber and C. F. Kemerer, A metrics suite for object oriented design, IEEE TSE 20, pp. 476-493, 1994
edges.evidence: the matched metrics in ant-1.3=>ar5 are the response for class (RFC: number of methods invoked by a class) [80] and the number of unique operands (unique operands) [4]

edges.target: Halstead metrics (unique operands)
edges.ref: [4] M. H. Halstead, Elements of Software Science, Elsevier, 1977
edges.evidence: The metrics used in both NASA and SOFTLAB groups are Halstead and McCabe's cyclomatic metrics

edges.target: Significance level 0.05 convention (Corder & Foreman)
edges.ref: [78] G. W. Corder and D. I. Foreman, Nonparametric Statistics for Non-Statisticians: A Step-by-Step Approach, Wiley, 2009
edges.evidence: we chose a cutoff of 0.05 which is a commonly accepted significance level in the statistical test [78].

edges.target: Dataset shift in SE prediction (Turhan)
edges.ref: [81] B. Turhan, On the dataset shift problem in software engineering prediction models, ESE 17(1-2), pp. 62-74, 2012
edges.evidence: HDP also addresses several issues related to a dataset shift such as the covariate shift and domain shift discussed by Turhan [81].

edges.target: Two-phase recommendation model (Kim, Tao, Kim, Zeller)
edges.ref: [79] D. Kim, Y. Tao, S. Kim, A. Zeller, Where should we fix this bug? a two-phase recommendation model, IEEE TSE 39(11), 2013
edges.evidence: our HDP approach follows a similar concept to the two-phase prediction model [79]: (1) checking prediction feasibility between source and target datasets, and (2) predicting defects.

edges.target: Logistic regression logit linearity explanation (Bruin, UCLA)
edges.ref: [83] J. Bruin. (2011, Feb.) newtest: command to compute new test, http://www.ats.ucla.edu/stat/stata/ado/analysis/
edges.evidence: The Logistic Regression models works well when there is a linear relationship between a predictor variable (a metric) and the logit transformation of the outcome variable [83].

edges.target: Learners used in defect prediction literature (Ghotra, McIntosh, Hassan)
edges.ref: [82] Ghotra, McIntosh, Hassan, Revisiting the impact of classification techniques on the performance of defect prediction models, ICSE 2015
edges.evidence: we built HDP models ... with various learners used in defect prediction literature such as Random Forest, BayesNet, SVM, J48 Decision Tree, Simple Logistic, and Logistic Model Trees (LMT) [1], [7], [8], [70], [71], [82].

edges.target: Simplified metric set CPDP (He, Li, Liu, Chen, Ma)
edges.ref: [44] P. He, B. Li, X. Liu, J. Chen, Y. Ma, An empirical study on software defect prediction with a simplified metric set, IST 59, pp. 170-190, 2015
edges.evidence: this result confirms the previous studies that we can build prediction models better than or comparable to WPDP models with even a few key metrics [44], [50].

not_reuse_examples: [45] Zhang et al. universal defect model: discussed in related work as inapplicable to heterogeneous metric sets, not run or compared against (only the median-chop premise is reused, captured separately).
[23]-[26] Posnett, Yang, Bettenburg, Menzies local-vs-global learning: motivation for transfer learning in Section 2 only; nothing from them is run, measured or adopted.
[37]-[41] Canfora, Panichella, Ryu, Zhang CPDP methods: listed as related same-metric-set CPDP work; none executed as baselines.
[17]-[22] IEEE 1012, Endres & Rombach, Jones, Glass, Budgen & Kitchenham: cited only to motivate the question of SE generality.
notes: Journal extension (TSE 2016) of Nam & Kim FSE'15 HDP; empirical CPDP study on 28 datasets/5 groups plus a sampling-size study and a Monte Carlo/decision-tree math model; many self-citations (Menzies, Kim, Nam); reference list truncated at [89], no [3]/[5] direct reuse.
